Language models are typically trained on extensive, static corpora, yet many real-world applications require training data that changes over time. For instance, news-based applications often require models to be trained on news articles that are continuously added to the dataset. This paper investigates the impact of data evolution on language models, specifically examining how well models trained on historical data perform on future data. We evaluate this performance using a state-of-the-art generative language model across multiple English text collections. Our findings reveal that generative models trained on historical data suffer significant performance degradation when tested on data from later time periods. We attribute this decline to a shift in the underlying data distribution, which we quantify by measuring the distance between distributions of consecutive data subsets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this distributional shift can be effectively captured by analyzing the representations of the language model itself.

Quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) are a frequent phenomenon observed in solar flares, yet their underlying physical mechanisms remain a subject of ongoing debate. This study examines a solar flare event that exhibited distinct QPPs in both hard X-ray (HXR) and radio emissions. The analysis focuses on a flare from the AR12673 region that occurred on 2014 September 6, utilizing data from the RHESSI and the Nobeyama Radio Observatory (NRO). The radio signal displayed a complex pattern of QPPs characterized by a dominant period of approximately 10 seconds, with secondary periods ranging from 1.5 to 3 seconds. Concurrently, the HXR data revealed a burst of QPPs with periods between 1 and 10 seconds. By applying a time-lag analysis to the radio and HXR signals, we determined that the radio and HXR emissions were nearly simultaneous, with the radio emission lagging by roughly 1 second. Furthermore, the radio and HXR intensities were found to be tightly correlated. These findings suggest that the radio and HXR emissions originate from the same physical processes, likely involving the same electron population. The results indicate that the radio and HXR QPPs are manifestations of the same physical mechanism, likely driven by magnetic reconnection occurring at a quasi-periodic rate.

This study introduces a novel approach for identifying anomalies in images by employing a conditional generative model. The proposed method, named GAD, utilizes a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to detect anomalies. The framework consists of two components: a discriminator that evaluates anomaly levels, and a conditional generator that learns the distribution of normal images. The discriminator distinguishes between normal and anomalous regions, while the conditional generator produces synthetic normal images based on input coordinates. The core concept involves feeding image coordinates into the trained generator; pixels where the output deviates significantly from the discriminator's assessment of normality are classified as anomalies. The methodology is evaluated on the MVTec-AD benchmark, demonstrating that GAD achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This paper investigates the Cauchy problem associated with dispersion-generalized Kadomtsev–Petviashvili I equations defined on the two-dimensional torus. It is established that strong dispersion ensures well-posedness in a weighted Sobolev space, where the exponent matches the regularity of the initial data.

This study examines a model of interacting fermions on a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice that preserves Kramers' time-reversal symmetry. The system features a two-body interaction characterized by a coupling strength that varies with the separation between fermions. The interaction strength is decomposed into a mean-field term and a fluctuating component. The analysis focuses on the ground-state phase diagram of this system, specifically investigating how it evolves as the fluctuations increase. The results demonstrate that the quantum phase transitions occurring at zero temperature are captured by mean-field theory, which treats the fluctuating interactions separately.

This paper introduces a deep learning-based channel prediction framework designed for millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive MIMO systems in high-mobility scenarios. The approach utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) to forecast future channel states by analyzing historical data. The study first establishes a channel model that accounts for both spatial and temporal correlations within mmWave channels. Subsequently, the paper develops a specific CNN architecture tailored to this channel model, integrating two key components: a channel decomposition module that aligns with the model's structure and a convolutional layer designed to capture temporal dependencies. Simulation results indicate that the proposed framework significantly outperforms existing methods, delivering a 10% improvement in prediction accuracy.

This study introduces a Bayesian framework for estimating income inequality at the microregional level, utilizing a small area regression model to link macro-level data with microregion-specific estimates. The approach employs the Gini coefficient alongside entropy-based measures of inequality. The proposed methodology is evaluated through a simulation study, followed by an application to the 2011 UK census data. The results demonstrate that the method effectively captures the known patterns of income inequality across different microregions.

This paper presents an explicit formula for the kernel of the Fourier transform defined on the Grauert tube of a manifold $\mathcal{M}$, utilizing the Cauchy-Fueter transform. This formula is constructed through the Cauchy-Fueter transform acting on specific invariant forms derived from the Szeg\"{o} projector. Furthermore, we establish the explicit form of the kernel for the spherical Fourier transform on the sphere $S^m$, derived from the aforementioned kernel.

This study presents MARINLINGA, a new algorithm designed to calculate reverse updates for graph languages. It achieves a worst-case time complexity of $O(|E| \log |E|)$, where $|E|$ represents the number of edges in the input language graph. This represents an improvement over the previously established $O(|E| \log^2 |E|)$ complexity of the MRLUGA algorithm, which is a specialized reverse update procedure for graph languages. Furthermore, we demonstrate that MARINLINGA surpasses the $O(|E| \log |E|)$ worst-case time complexity of the recent forward update method, OREDACT, proposed by \cite{oredata}.

We demonstrate a coincidence between the associated roots of non-self-intersecting curves and real Schur roots, and we establish that the associated roots of an irreducible curve correspond to a simple real Schur module. Software applications frequently rely on numerous packages, yet developers often import unnecessary dependencies, leading to bloated code that complicates maintenance and increases vulnerability to security breaches. This study introduces a novel technique to identify such superfluous dependencies by leveraging the execution traces of a software system. We present a new algorithm that pinpoints dependencies not utilized during trace operations. Furthermore, we evaluate the efficacy of this approach using a comprehensive suite of real-world Java applications. The results demonstrate that the method successfully recovers dependencies absent in trace execution, thereby offering a robust mechanism for detecting and eliminating unnecessary imports.

This study investigates a model of two-dimensional polymer chains that interact solely through kinship. The degree of kinship is determined by the extent of overlap between chains; for instance, a higher probability of two chains sharing a common ancestor correlates with greater overlap likelihood. We examine the statistical properties of these abstract chains using both analytical methods and Monte Carlo simulations. Our findings indicate that, as chain length increases, the system's behavior can be characterized by a single order parameter. Furthermore, a distinct phase transition occurs at a specific critical value for the kinship probability.

This paper investigates multistage distributionally robust optimization (DRO) under uncertainty, specifically examining the impact of restricting scenario paths. While prior research has extensively addressed multistage DRO without path restrictions, this work introduces a generalized framework for modeling such constraints. We define a generalized multistage DRO problem where scenario paths are selected from a predefined collection of paths, each characterized by a specific cost. This formulation extends the classic multistage DRO problem by incorporating path costs and is applicable to various practical contexts, such as supply chain planning with limited operational modes and financial portfolio optimization with restricted strategies. We establish that the Generalized Multistage DRO problem is NP-hard, even when restricted to a single stage. Furthermore, we propose a two-stage algorithm that leverages the L-shaped method to solve the first-stage optimization and employs a tailored Benders decomposition for the second stage. Numerical experiments demonstrate the proposed approach's effectiveness on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

This study introduces a novel framework for predicting future video characteristics and actions. The approach utilizes a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to synthesize future video data and a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to extract features from these sequences for action classification. By integrating the RNN-generated video features with CNN features from the initial frames, the system effectively captures both temporal and spatial dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate that this method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of accuracy.

We examine the emergence of thermalization within closed quantum many-body systems, specifically focusing on the impact of weak interactions. By utilizing a perturbative approach, we derive an effective Hamiltonian for a non-interacting fermionic system subject to small perturbations. This Hamiltonian encapsulates the influence of weak interactions, allowing us to analyze the time-evolution of the system's state. Our analysis reveals that the resulting state exhibits "deep thermalization," meaning the system reaches a thermal state even for observables that are not local. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the thermalization process occurs on a timescale that is merely logarithmic with respect to the system's Hilbert space dimension.

This paper examines properties of pseudo-differential operators defined on homogeneous trees. We define a symbol class $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{T}_d)$ for the non-separable tree $\mathbb{T}_d$ with degree $d\geq 3$, and establish that an operator $T_{f}$ with symbol $f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{T}_d)$ is bounded. The rapid expansion of 5G networks has sparked significant public concern regarding the potential health risks associated with their electromagnetic (EM) emissions. This study aims to quantify the EM exposure from 5G radio base stations (RBS) and smartphones to evaluate whether a safety gap exists between them. Our analysis covers two main areas: first, a review of the current 5G network landscape in Germany, focusing on the frequency bands utilized by 5G operators; and second, an assessment of EM exposure from both RBS and smartphones. To achieve this, we employed a ray-tracing method to calculate RBS exposure and a 3D anthropomorphic model to simulate smartphone exposure. Our findings indicate that overall EM exposure from smartphones exceeds that of RBS, particularly at the 28 GHz band, where smartphone exposure is 1.5 to 2.5 times higher than RBS exposure. Furthermore, we identified a strong correlation between the density of 5G RBS and the EM exposure from smartphones. Consequently, our results suggest that current regulatory limits are not being met in cases where users rely on 5G smartphones.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) often produce overconfident results on out-of-distribution (OOD) samples, a behavior that poses significant risks in safety-critical applications. To address this, we introduce the concept of OOD Certificates (CODEs)—adversarial examples that cause a DNN to incorrectly classify a new input as its correct class. By examining how CODEs interact with a model's output, we can generate reliable OOD Certificates. Our findings demonstrate that CODEs outperform existing baselines in generating more precise certificates, thereby offering a more trustworthy mechanism for detecting OOD samples.

This study presents an analysis of the azimuthal correlations between the leading and sub-leading jets in $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 7$ TeV, utilizing the ALICE detector at the LHC. The analysis focuses on events with a high transverse momentum trigger jet ($p_{\rm T}^{\rm trig} > 30$ GeV/$c$) and a lower activity associated jet ($p_{\rm T}^{\rm assoc} > 20$ MeV/$c$) within the central pseudorapidity region ($| \eta | < 0.8$). The measured sensitivity of these azimuthal jet correlations to the event plane is evaluated across three distinct ranges of the associated jet's transverse momentum.

Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in numerous domains, including image classification, object detection, and speech recognition. However, the primary limitation of these models is their dependence on vast amounts of labeled data. To address this, the study introduces a novel deep learning framework that leverages unlabeled data through semi-supervised and unsupervised techniques to enhance performance. The proposed approach employs a dual-stream architecture, where the first stream utilizes labeled data to train a feature extractor, and the second stream processes unlabeled data to generate pseudo-labels. These pseudo-labels subsequently refine the model's accuracy. The methodology was evaluated on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets, demonstrating that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art models.

This study introduces a novel approach to outlier detection that leverages the reconstruction error of an autoencoder. By training the autoencoder on a dataset of unlabeled normal instances, the method identifies outliers based on their elevated reconstruction errors when processed against the learned normal distribution. Experimental results demonstrate that utilizing these features significantly enhances the efficacy of outlier detection. Furthermore, we illustrate that this strategy can be integrated with existing detection techniques to boost their performance. The proposed method is demonstrated to yield superior outcomes compared to current state-of-the-art approaches.

This work investigates the non-linear equation
$$ u(t) + \int_0^t (t-y)^\alpha A u(y) dy = f(t), \quad t \ge 0, $$
where the operator $A$ represents an unbounded sectorial operator within a Banach space, and the function $f$ is a given function. We establish that if $\alpha$ adheres to specific constraints and $f$ adheres to particular regularity conditions, then the equation possesses a unique "mild" solution that is also a classical solution.

The brain's intricate architecture and function are defined by a complex web of interactions among neurons, glial cells, and various specialized cell types. In this study, we examine how neuron-glial dynamics influence neural network activity. We introduce a model where glial cells regulate the firing rates of neuronal populations through a nonlinear, saturating mechanism. Our findings indicate that this regulation can generate novel, large-scale synchronized states within networks, even in parameter regimes where individual neurons remain in a critical state. These emergent synchronized states are characterized by a collective, neuron-by-neuron reduction in firing rates. We demonstrate that such a synchronized regime can expand significantly, encompassing a substantial portion of the overall phase space.

This study investigates the quantum tunneling of a neutral spin-½ particle through a double-slit barrier situated within a magnetic vortex field. We derive the energy spectrum and the corresponding energy eigenfunctions for this system. Furthermore, we examine the influence of the particle's spin on its spatial probability distribution.

This study examines the fluctuation theory of first passage times for a Brownian particle within an oscillating boundary. We derive an explicit formula for the probability density function governing the event of a particle touching the boundary for the nth time. Furthermore, we calculate the nth-order moment of this distribution and illustrate the process with several specific examples.

We demonstrate that the formal semigroup associated with an L-space knot is completely determined by the expansion of its Alexander polynomial. Furthermore, we show that specific algebraic invariants derived from these semigroups correspond to topological characteristics of the knot complement. Specifically, we establish that the multiplicity of the leading term in an L-space knot's Alexander polynomial matches the multiplicity of the first non-vanishing term in its knot Floer $ ar{H}_ ar$omology. Additionally, we prove that the multiplicity of the trailing term in the polynomial equals the number of components in the link formed by taking the $+1$-surgery on the knot.

This study demonstrates that the evolution of a compressible three-dimensional viscous fluid, initially close to a stationary state, is governed in the inviscid limit by the compressible Euler equations. This result, which applies without assuming small initial perturbations, holds for either the isentropic or full compressible Navier-Stokes equations. The analysis further incorporates initial data that may be merely $L^2$ in the initial condition and allows for a $t^{1/2}$ asymptotic profile in the perturbation, which is only applicable to the full compressible Navier-Stokes framework.

This study introduces an ensemble deep-learning approach designed to enhance object detection performance. The proposed method integrates the predictive outputs of multiple detectors, each trained on distinct object detection datasets. By utilizing a subsequent detector to aggregate these individual predictions, the system effectively mitigates the weaknesses inherent in single-detector models. Experimental results demonstrate that this strategy yields a significant improvement in detection accuracy.

Identifiers are fundamental to programming languages, yet their naming conventions vary significantly across projects. This study analyzes the nomenclature of identifiers in Python by examining how linguistic structures differ among variables, functions, classes, and attributes based on their roles. By applying clustering techniques to training data derived from a comprehensive repository of 1,000+ open-source projects, we identified distinct naming patterns for each identifier type. Furthermore, we developed an ensemble model capable of predicting the identifier type based on its name. Evaluation results indicate that the model achieves an F1-score of 0.92, with individual scores of 0.97 or higher for each specific category.

Consider the unital associative algebra generated by elements $e_{ij}$ for $1 \leq i, j \leq n$, subject to the relations $e_{ij}e_{kl} = \delta_{j,k} e_{i,l}$ and the constraint $\sum_{k=1}^n e_{ik} = \sum_{k=1}^n e_{ki} = e_{ii}$ for all $i$. We refer to a vector $v$ in the $n$-dimensional vector space $V$ as NIL if, for every $i$, the condition $e_{ii}v = v e_{ii} = 0$ holds. The primary objective of this paper is to establish the condition under which a vector $v$ belongs to the subspace spanned by NIL vectors.

The study employs a phase-field approach to simulate grain growth in duplex and triplex microstructures, examining how the growth of individual phases influences the overall evolution. By utilizing a modified phase-field model incorporating a gradient energy term, the authors demonstrate that phase evolution is governed by either the volume fraction or the interfacial area fraction, depending on the specific phase composition. Findings indicate that the overall kinetics are driven by the phase with the lowest interface energy rather than the one with the largest volume fraction. Furthermore, the research reveals that the growth rate of the dominant phase increases as the volume fraction of the minor phase rises, whereas the growth of the minor phase is accelerated by the presence of the dominant phase. These results are attributed to the differing interfacial energies between phases, which dictate the overall growth kinetics.

Accurate 3D human pose and shape estimation is essential for numerous applications, including augmented reality, virtual reality, and human-computer interaction. Despite significant advancements, current models still face challenges in robustness and precision. This study identifies two key factors that substantially influence model performance: the quality of the training data and the effectiveness of the training strategy. To address data quality, we introduce a new dataset derived from 2D-to-3D pose conversion, featuring 10,000 annotated samples. This resource is designed to enhance the generalization capabilities of 3D estimation models. Regarding the training strategy, we propose a novel loss function that integrates both 3D joint distances and linear regression errors, offering a more effective learning mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches on the challenging 3D Human Pose Estimation 2018 (HPE2018) dataset, achieving a Mean Per-Joint Position Error (MPJPE) of 65.82 mm and an Procrustes Fit Error (PFE) of 52.02 mm.

We introduce a theoretical framework for superconductivity in dilute electron systems featuring localized negative U-centers. In this model, superconducting pairing is mediated by the same centers responsible for the negative U-value, and the associated energy gap is derived from the ground-state energy difference of a two-site system. Our analysis indicates that the negative exponent of this ground-state energy difference governs the temperature-dependent energy gap, which in turn dictates the superconducting critical temperature. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the ground-state wave function exhibits a spatially oscillatory character, implying that the order parameter possesses a finite momentum. Numerical results for the single-impurity Andreev reflection coefficient reveal a pronounced temperature dependence, which increases with the density of impurities. Additionally, we calculate the local density of states and the local density of states for quasiparticles, showing that both are sensitive to both temperature and the density of impurities.

Scalar leptoquarks are a prominent class of hypothetical particles that have attracted significant interest within both theoretical and experimental particle physics. This study introduces a new methodology for analyzing the differential cross sections of leptoquark production and subsequent decay into a quark and a lepton, specifically examining scenarios where the lepton is identified via a charged or neutral current. The derived analytical formulas are valid for any arbitrary center-of-mass energy and leptoquark mass, as well as for any leptoquark mass and any lepton and quark flavor. Additionally, the paper provides specific formulas for the center-of-mass frame, which are particularly useful for describing the production of heavy leptoquarks in high-energy neutrino-nucleon collisions.

In the last ten years, machine learning has become a dominant force in computer science, while category theory has emerged as a powerful framework for modeling computational processes. Recently, the integration of these fields has gained significant traction, with numerous researchers exploring machine learning through categorical lens. This paper surveys the recent advancements at the intersection of machine learning and category theory, alongside outlining open questions and potential future pathways.

This paper introduces a novel terminal sliding mode control (TSMC) algorithm for second-order Newtonian dynamics featuring a measurable output state, $y$, distinct from the system's state, $x$. The proposed approach ensures finite-time convergence of $y$ to the reference trajectory $y_d$ without requiring $y_d$ to be constant. The method relies on the assumption that $y$ is a linear function of $x$ with a known transformation matrix. The study demonstrates that the optimal power ratio for the measurable output in this dynamic configuration is 0.5, a value that significantly enhances convergence speed and control precision compared to existing TSMC variants. Theoretical proofs establish the stability of the proposed system, and the effectiveness of the approach is validated through simulations on a two-link robotic manipulator.

Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are essential components in modern society, but their widespread use necessitates non-destructive methods to assess internal health. While current techniques like X-ray computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offer detailed internal insights, they are hindered by slow acquisition speeds and poor spatial resolution. This study introduces a novel approach combining a deep learning framework with a new imaging modality called nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMRs). Unlike traditional MRI, which relies on spatial encoding, NMRs capture the frequency spectrum of NMR signals, providing a unique way to characterize internal structures. The proposed deep learning model effectively translates NMRs data into a spatially resolved image of the internal LIB architecture. The method's performance was validated using a physical prototype, demonstrating its capability to reconstruct internal structures. Furthermore, the technique was applied to quantify lithium-ion concentration within an aged battery cell, successfully identifying localized degradation patterns.

This paper introduces a discrete-time tracking control strategy for a gantry system, designed to enhance tracking precision and circumvent the challenges associated with classical continuous-time methods. The approach utilizes a discrete model derived via the first principles of motion, incorporating discrete-time state and output feedback. The controller's robustness is validated through simulations and experiments, demonstrating superior performance in handling both parametric uncertainties and unmodeled dynamics.

Image captioning systems have advanced significantly, yet they remain constrained by the scarcity of high-quality, large-scale datasets. This study introduces the CRAFT framework, which utilizes a caption dataset comprising 100 million entries derived from crowdsourced and automated sources. The system employs a two-stage approach: first, it trains a model to generate captions from images, followed by a refinement process that leverages weak supervision to enhance caption quality. This approach yields a new dataset of 100 million human-annotated captions that substantially outperforms previous datasets. Experiments demonstrate that CRAFT-based models achieve state-of-the-art results on the COCO benchmark and establish new capabilities for generating long-tail captions. The dataset and source code are publicly accessible at https://github.com/Alibaba-ML-SYSTEM/CRAFT.

A collection $S$ of strings is defined as well-connected if, for any two distinct strings $s_1, s_2 \in S$, there exists a sequence $s_1, \dots, s_k$ of strings within $S$ such that every intermediate string $s_i$ (for $1 < i < k$) shares a non-empty intersection with both its immediate neighbors, $s_{i-1}$ and $s_{i+1}$. This paper demonstrates that for any finite set $S$ of non-empty words, there exists a non-empty sub-collection $S' \subseteq S$ that is well-connected, with the length of this sub-collection bounded by $O(\max\{|s| : s \in S\})$. Additionally, we examine the scenario where $S$ consists of $n$-element subsets of an alphabet $\Sigma$, treating these subsets as $| \Sigma |$-length strings where character occurrences match element frequency. We prove that for any such finite collection $S$, there is a subset $S' \subseteq S$ of size $n$ that is well-connected, with the maximum cardinality of $S'$ being $O(|\Sigma|)$.

Ehresmann semigroups are subcategories of binary semilattices that have been thoroughly examined, with their order properties extensively documented in existing works. This paper presents ordered Ehresmann semigroups as special instances of semilattice-ordered structures and examines their fundamental characteristics.

Self-attention architectures have become the standard in natural language processing, yet their theoretical understanding remains incomplete. This paper investigates the expressive power of these architectures by examining the relationship between network width, depth, and width. We demonstrate that a constant-width, constant-depth network is insufficient to represent certain functions that can be achieved by increasing the network's depth. Furthermore, we show that a constant-width, constant-depth network is insufficient to represent certain functions that can be achieved by increasing the network's width. This study reports the synthesis of BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles (NPs) via a sol-gel method, utilizing a citric acid-to-metal precursor ratio of 3:1. The NPs were fabricated at temperatures ranging from 160$^{\circ}$C to 500$^{\circ}$C. Structural and morphological analyses, including X-ray diffraction (XRD), Raman spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), confirmed that the samples exhibited a rhombohedral structure with a single perovskite phase. Notably, the nanoparticle samples produced at 160$^{\circ}$C exhibited a significantly higher specific surface area compared to the bulk material. These 160$^{\circ}$C-synthesized NPs were evaluated for their photocatalytic performance in degrading Rhodamine B (RhB) under UV light irradiation. Results indicated that the NPs generated at 160$^{\circ}$C achieved a 90% degradation of RhB within 120 minutes, outperforming the bulk material, which only reached 60% degradation in the same timeframe. This enhanced performance is attributed to the elevated specific surface area and the absence of crystal defects in the low-temperature NPs.

We introduce a model featuring a $Z_2$-symmetric extension of the Standard Model, where the $Z_2$-invariant condition requires the Higgs potential's minimum to align with a vacuum expectation value (vev) of a single Higgs doublet. This setup permits a residual $Z_2$-symmetry at the electroweak scale, which can be broken by a small vacuum misalignment. This misalignment induces a non-zero coupling between the Higgs boson and dark matter, allowing the Higgs to serve as the primary decay channel for dark matter. Consequently, the model predicts a specific relationship between the dark matter relic density and its coupling strength to the Higgs boson.

This study addresses the challenge of reconstructing hand-held objects from a single RGB image. We contend that the dynamic nature of hand gestures significantly influences the object's appearance, a factor often overlooked in prior research. To address this, we introduce a new framework that simultaneously estimates the object's shape, the hand's configuration, and the object's 6D pose. Our approach begins by generating a coarse 3D object shape through a 2D-3D CNN, followed by refining it using a differentiable rendering process that incorporates hand-object interactions. Specifically, we employ a differentiable physics engine to model how hands and held objects interact physically, enabling the joint optimization of both object shape and hand poses. Experiments on the HO3D dataset demonstrate that this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study introduces a new method for deriving sunspot umbral temperatures from ground-based photospheric observations, specifically utilizing the Equal Contrast technique. This approach is validated by comparing it with independent temperature measurements derived from solar Ca-K line observations. The analysis reveals that the correlation between traditional umbral photospheric data and Ca-K line observations is weak, whereas the Equal Contrast method demonstrates a significantly stronger correlation. The findings indicate that the Equal Contrast technique more accurately reflects the physical temperature of sunspot umbrae.

This study reports a search for the decay $\Sigma^+\to\pi^+\pi^0$ using $\Sigma^+$ samples from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, recorded by the LHCb detector. The analysis utilizes an integrated luminosity of 9 fb$^{-1}$, focusing on a signal region where the $\pi^0$ decays into two photons. Researchers identified 10 candidate events, a count that exceeds the 2.1 expected background events, yielding a significance of 5.0 standard deviations. This result represents the first observation of this decay mode. The observed branching fraction is $(4.9\pm 1.1\pm 0.4)\times 10^{-9}$, with uncertainties quoted for statistical and systematic sources respectively. The finding aligns with prior theoretical predictions and existing measurements.

Distributed symbolic execution (SE) is a technique for automatically exploring the state space of a program by dividing the workload across multiple machines. However, current partitioning strategies often fail to ensure that each machine receives a sufficiently large portion of the search space, resulting in underutilized resources. This study introduces a test-depth partitioning strategy designed to distribute the search space equitably. By estimating execution paths based on their depth, test-depth partitioning assigns tasks to machines so that each is burdened with an equal number of paths. We evaluated this approach against existing partitioning methods using a suite of programs from the Daikon suite. Results demonstrate that test-depth partitioning achieves superior load balancing, leading to improved resource utilization and enhanced overall performance.

This study examines how the aspect ratio of magnetic nanoparticles influences their relaxation dynamics, specifically within a dipolar interaction regime. We analyze both the short-range and long-range behaviors of the correlation function, which are governed by different physical mechanisms. Our findings indicate that at low dipolar interaction strengths, the correlation function's decay is primarily dictated by the particle shape ratio, whereas at high interaction strengths, the behavior is predominantly controlled by the magnetic dipolar forces.

However, the reliance of FL on communication between clients and a central server introduces significant risks, including latency and potential privacy breaches. To mitigate these issues, we introduce a privacy-preserving FL framework that leverages a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) to secure the communication channel between the server and clients. This framework operates in two modes: a standard mode for open networks and a secure mode for open networks. Short-text classification is a prevalent challenge in natural language processing, with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) being a popular choice for handling sequential data. However, existing RNN-based methods often overlook the importance of context, which is crucial for understanding the meaning of a short text. To address this, we introduce a new approach that integrates a context-aware mechanism into RNNs for classification. Our method employs a context-aware attention module to capture dependencies between the current word and its surrounding environment, enabling the network to learn more effective representations. Experimental results on two datasets demonstrate that this approach outperforms current state-of-the-art short-text classification methods.

This study examines the sensitivity of the electric field in Fabry-P\'{e}rot etalons, specifically analyzing how the field responds to changes in optical thickness. We introduce a new analytical approach to evaluate this sensitivity, which is critical for the development of advanced etalons for applications like gravitational wave detection. Our analysis reveals that the electric field can be decomposed into a component that remains insensitive to thickness variations and a set of components that are highly sensitive. We demonstrate that by utilizing a specific set of initial field amplitudes, one can isolate the insensitive portion, thereby nullifying the effects of thickness fluctuations. This methodology is particularly valuable for enhancing the stability of Fabry-P\'{e}rot etalons.

A matching $M$ defined on $2n$ points is compatible if it can be realized by a single geometric arrangement of $n$ convex shapes. For two convex shapes $C_1$ and $C_2$, each containing $n$ labeled vertices, a matching is compatible precisely when it respects the cyclic orderings of their boundaries. This paper establishes that any compatible matching between such labeled convex shapes contains at most $\lfloor 3n/2 \rfloor$ edges. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this upper bound is tight for all $n \ge 2$. Finally, we examine compatible matchings within a single set of $n$ convex shapes, proving that the maximum number of edges in such a configuration is exactly $n-1$.

Chiplet technology offers a solution to the challenges of integrating multiple vendor-produced dies into a single chip by utilizing an interconnect standard to connect them. Although the industry has established several standards, such as Intel's Intel EMIB and Ultra-Fine Interconnect (UFI), these often fail to account for the specific needs of the software running on the chiplet. This paper introduces the concept of a "Software-Defined Chiplet," which aims to address the critical issue of software interoperability. We present a novel framework designed to facilitate the creation of software-optimized chiplet systems, which includes a proposed interface for capturing the software requirements of these chiplet designs. Furthermore, we introduce a novel method for assessing the performance of these chiplet interfaces, which is demonstrated through a case study on the software requirements of the AMD Firefly chiplet. Finally, we evaluate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to a real-world scenario involving the software of the AMD Firefly chiplet.

Mixture cure models are designed to evaluate the impact of covariates on the probability of long-term survival and the hazard rate for uncured individuals. This paper introduces a novel framework for fitting such models that incorporates a latent Gaussian random effects structure, allowing for the simultaneous analysis of censored and uncured subjects. By leveraging the Bayesian methodology, the proposed approach offers a robust and flexible tool for modeling survival data, particularly when dealing with complex data patterns. The study demonstrates the efficacy of this new method through simulation experiments and a real-world application.

The nonlocal metric dimension of a graph $G$, denoted as $\text{dim}_{\text{non}}(G)$, is defined as the cardinality of a nonlocal resolving set for $G$. A subset $W$ of the vertex set $V(G)$ constitutes a nonlocal resolving set if, for any two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$ in $G$, there exists at least one $w \in W$ such that the nonlocal distance $d_{\text{non}}(w, u)$ differs from $d_{\text{non}}(w, v$; here, $d_{\text{non}}(w, u)$ represents the minimal common distance from $w$ to any vertex in the shortest path connecting $u$ and $v$. A nonlocal metric dimension is attained by the smallest possible nonlocal resolving set, while a nonlocal metric basis comprises a corresponding minimal set. This study establishes several key findings: first, it derives the nonlocal metric dimensions for both complete graphs and path graphs; second, it provides characterizations of trees possessing a nonlocal metric dimension of either 1 or 2; and third, it proves that the complete bipartite graph $K_{m,n}$, where $m \leq n$, achieves a nonlocal metric dimension of $m$.

In-memory computing systems, which fuse memory and processing units, offer a promising avenue for accelerating deep neural networks (DNNs). However, their performance is often constrained by the low precision of analog memory devices. To address this, we introduce a novel training framework for DNNs that leverages the inherent characteristics of these memory hardware components. Our approach employs a specialized hardware-aware loss function to embed the properties of the memory system directly into the training process. Furthermore, we develop a new training strategy that dynamically adjusts the loss function parameters to match the specific hardware architecture. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across various in-memory DNNs, with a significant advantage of requiring no extra memory or compute resources.

Seismic data denoising is a critical task in seismic processing, and deep learning has emerged as a leading method for this purpose. However, supervised deep learning approaches are heavily dependent on the availability of clean, noise-free training data, which is rarely accessible in real-world scenarios. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel deep learning framework for seismic denoising that utilizes noisy data exclusively. This approach employs a dual-stream architecture: one stream extracts features from clean data via an autoencoder, while the other stream processes noisy data through a separate network. These streams are integrated within a gated fusion module, which is optimized using a hybrid loss function combining mean square error and spectral norm constraints. Experiments conducted on both synthetic and field data demonstrate that this method effectively suppresses noise while preserving essential signal characteristics, achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art denoising techniques.

The JLab experiment E00-004-090, conducted on a deuterium target, investigated two-photon exchange effects in elastic lepton scattering by measuring the differential cross sections of positrons and electrons scattered from deuterons at backward angles. Utilizing data from both electron and positron beams, researchers achieved the first direct observation of the two-photon exchange phenomenon in scattering. The experiment operated at beam energies of 6.0 and 8.0 GeV, covering positron scattering angles between 120° and 160° with a beam current of 100 µA. The Hubbard model serves as a foundational framework for describing strongly correlated electrons or holes within antiferromagnetic lattices, where substantial on-site Coulomb repulsion prevents double occupancy of a single site. In this work, we investigate the strong-coupling regime of the Hubbard model using a variational approach based on the Gutzwiller approximation. We derive an approximate analytical form for the free energy and analyze the phase diagram, specifically focusing on the influence of strong correlations on the superconducting phase. Our analysis reveals that strong-coupling superconductivity can manifest in three distinct ways: (i) within a metallic region, (ii) as a Mott-insulator-to-Metal transition accompanied by superconductivity, or (iii) as a Mott-insulator-to-Superconductor transition. Furthermore, we examine the temperature-dependent behavior of the superconducting gap and identify the corresponding critical temperatures.

Mediation analysis is a versatile method for identifying causal mechanisms, a field that has seen significant recent interest. This paper presents a new mediation model designed to estimate the mediating effect of multiple mediators within a unified framework. We establish the theoretical foundations for our approach, including the identification conditions and asymptotic properties of the resulting estimators. Furthermore, we develop a confidence interval for the causal mediation effect by applying the Gaussian approximation inherent in our asymptotic analysis. To evaluate the proposed method's performance, a simulation study is conducted, followed by an application of our technique to data from a clinical trial concerning the treatment of COVID-19.

The Starshade is a proposed space-based instrument designed to block light from bright stars, enabling the detection of faint nearby exoplanets. This paper introduces a new method for estimating the Strehl ratio of the Starshade using a single, low-resolution, off-axis intensity measurement from a distant guide star. The approach relies on a machine learning model trained on simulated data, which correlates the observed intensity with the Strehl ratio. We evaluate the technique's performance across various starshade configurations and demonstrate its efficacy in recovering Strehl ratios from actual on-orbit data.

Suicide remains a significant global challenge, causing substantial loss of life, and the primary obstacle to effective prevention is the delayed recognition of suicidal intent. This paper introduces a novel approach to identifying early warning signs by leveraging social media data, utilizing a deep learning framework designed to pinpoint text segments that signal such intent. The study evaluates various deep learning architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and assesses their performance using standard metrics like precision, recall, and F1-score. The results indicate that the proposed method achieves an F1-score of 0.71, outperforming existing baseline approaches.

We have constructed a formulation for supersymmetric Schwarzians applicable to any superconformal group of three dimensions. This construction utilizes the technique of embedding superconformal groups within global spacetime symmetries, thereby deriving the associated one-form connections and their curvature constraints. The resulting supersymmetric Schwarzians serve as the foundational components for the chiral 2-form fields that characterize superconformal geometry.

This study examines discrete dynamical systems defined by difference equations of order four, specifically those featuring a nonlinear term and a 1/Ladai difference structure. The analysis focuses on the system's qualitative dynamics, particularly whether solutions oscillate, diverge, or converge. The findings presented here are derived from a combination of original research and computational simulations.

This work examines the dynamics of a Born-Infeld model within nonlinear electrodynamics, specifically focusing on its interaction with a constant uniform external magnetic field. By employing the method of exact memetic solutions, the authors derive an analytical description of the resulting system's energy density. Furthermore, the study investigates the equation of state, highlighting its transition from a non-relativistic to a relativistic regime.

This study examines the magnetic susceptibility of the one-dimensional quantum XY model on a square lattice. The analysis reveals that, in the zero-temperature limit, the susceptibility follows a power law with respect to the transverse magnetic field, where the exponent is determined by the critical value of the field. The results also indicate that, in the high-temperature regime, the susceptibility approaches a constant value independent of the transverse magnetic field.

The Arrhenius law, which describes the temperature dependence of reaction rates, is a cornerstone of chemical kinetics. However, in this study, we demonstrate that the emergence of a non-thermal bath can cause a "hotter-faster" scenario, where a system with a higher initial temperature reaches equilibrium more rapidly than one starting from a cooler state. This behavior is observed in a model featuring a two-level system coupled to a bath with two-level energy levels, where the equilibrium time is found to be shorter for the hotter initial condition. This phenomenon is attributed to the energy exchange mechanism between the two-level system and the non-thermal bath, which accelerates relaxation in hot initial states.

This study examines quantum walks of dimer pairs in one-dimensional quasicrystalline structures where hopping follows a power-law decay. The analysis covers both repulsive and attractive pairwise interactions and reveals that localization is governed by the interplay between these factors and the algebraic decay of hopping amplitudes. Specifically, for repulsive interactions, the pair localization length follows a power-law scaling with the single-particle localization length. In contrast, attractive interactions lead to a phase diagram where the dimer localization length exhibits exponential growth with respect to single-particle localization length.

Task-oriented dialogue systems (TODs) are essential for supporting users in executing specific tasks, such as booking appointments or making reservations. However, current T-O-Ds are typically designed for a single language, resulting in restricted linguistic coverage. To address this, we introduce a novel T-O-D framework that supports multiple languages. This system utilizes a pre-trained encoder to leverage the multilingual capabilities of the encoder for cross-lingual transfer learning. We evaluate our approach on a multilingual version of the RESTAURANT-17C dataset, which encompasses four languages: English, German, French, and Spanish. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework outperforms existing methods, achieving a relative improvement of 10.4% over the baseline model.

Alternative splicing is a fundamental biological process that generates various protein variants from a single gene, and its dysregulation is strongly linked to numerous diseases, including cancer. This study introduces a novel computational framework for identifying alternative splicing abnormalities in cancer by integrating multiple data sources. The approach utilizes a multi-view Gaussian graphical model to construct a network that captures the interplay between alternative splicing patterns and gene expression levels. By applying this model, we construct a splicing-associated gene network to pinpoint genes involved in splicing misregulation. Furthermore, we develop a specific algorithm for network pruning that isolates cancer-related genes by leveraging known cancer driver genes. Experimental validation using data from 10 cancer types demonstrates that this method successfully identifies genes with high cancer relevance, and the resulting networks reveal distinct biological pathways and mechanisms driving various cancers.

We introduce a fresh approach to the HBT interferometry framework, designed to analyze particle production within the framework of the Color Glass Condensate. This methodology enables the investigation of how the 3-dipole correlator influences two-particle correlations.

This work examines the production of light nuclei in nuclear collisions, highlighting the coexistence of two production mechanisms: hard scattering and parton coalescence. We introduce a novel coalescence model that incorporates the momentum dependence of the nucleon phase-space density, which is a defining characteristic of the partonic stage. Our calculations, performed using the PHSD transport theory, are benchmarked against experimental data for both inclusive spectra and correlation functions. The results demonstrate that hard scattering and coalescence are essential for accurately describing both spectra and correlations. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that these correlations primarily arise from the coalescence mechanism, with the observed patterns serving as a sensitive probe of the phase-space density at the time of nucleon formation.

The fate of exoplanets with rocky compositions and primordial hydrogen-helium atmospheres remains uncertain. While high temperatures during the early stages of a star's life can drive atmospheric escape, this process is often insufficient to strip the envelope entirely. This study investigates the potential for subsequent atmospheric escape driven by the planet's own internal heat. We developed a one-dimensional model to simulate the evolution of a rocky planet's envelope, accounting for heat conduction from the interior and radiative cooling from the atmosphere. Our findings indicate that the envelope can persist for billions of years if the planet possesses a substantial heat flux. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the rate of atmospheric escape is governed by the rate at which the planet radiates its internal heat. Consequently, we estimate that approximately 10% of rocky planets with masses exceeding 10 Earth masses and orbital periods under 10 days would lose their envelopes over a 10-billion-year timeframe.

A graph $G$ is termed *$k$-dispersable* if it admits a vertex ordering such that its matching number does not exceed $k$ times its maximum degree. This paper demonstrates that for any graph $G$ with maximum degree $\Delta(G)$ and $n$ vertices, there exists a subgraph $H$ such that $G/H$ is $k$-dispersable, where the number of contracted vertices in $H$ is bounded by $\max\{k, \Delta(G)\}$. Additionally, it is established that for any graph $G$ with maximum degree $\Delta(G)$ and treewidth $k$, there exists a subgraph $H$ such that $G/H$ is $(k+\Delta(G))$-dispersable.

This paper introduces a novel iterative algorithm for matrix inversion that leverages the matrix exponential. It demonstrates that this approach offers superior numerical stability and lower complexity compared to traditional direct inversion techniques, thereby making it particularly advantageous for embedded systems. Additionally, the study provides a thorough analysis of the algorithm's computational complexity and evaluates its numerical behavior through various numerical experiments.

This paper investigates the dynamics of curvature perturbions within a novel two-field inflation framework. The model incorporates a "ultra slow roll" phase, driven by two fields with nearly orthogonal kinetic and potential contributions, to generate significant fluctuations in the curvature perturbation. The evolution proceeds from an initial quasi-single-field, nearly de Sitter epoch, transitions through a brief ultra slow roll phase, before concluding in standard slow roll inflation. We demonstrate that this mechanism can generate a substantial power spectrum amplitude, reaching values as high as $10^{-2}$, while maintaining consistency with current observational limits.

This study examines a refined version of the assortment optimization problem, which involves a retailer setting a price for each product in a potential collection to maximize revenue. This approach extends the classic problem, which assumes fixed product prices and focuses solely on selecting the optimal set. We introduce an efficient rounding algorithm that leverages a linear program (LP) relaxation to generate a high-quality assortment. Additionally, we prove that this method achieves a constant-factor approximation for both instances where the optimal option set is known in advance and those that must be discovered. We also demonstrate the method's effectiveness through numerical experiments.

The logistic distribution, which is a member of the Pearson VII family, is used to model the parametric hazard function, which is a known member of the Pearson family of distributions. The computation of three-loop mixed electrowlectweak and QCD corrections, as wellas pure three-wea k QCD corrections, remains a significant challenge in the study of two-body scattering processes within the Standard Model. This difficulty stems from the necessity of evaluating complex Feynman integrals, which are typically addressed using differential equations. This paper outlines a method for solving such equations, specifically for cases where the squared invariant mass of the outgoing particles serves as the variable. By employing a differential equation approach, we successfully derive the pure real part of the three-loop massive box diagram.

High-performance object stores (POS) have emerged as a promising alternative to traditional file systems for High-Performance Computing (HPC) storage, offering superior scalability and capacity. However, the absence of a POSIX-compatible interface and the lack of support for metadata-based access present significant hurdles for integrating them with current HPC software. To address this, we introduce a novel library that enables seamless metadata-based access to POSIX-compatible objects, designed to bridge the gap between legacy HPC software and modern storage infrastructure. By leveraging this library, researchers can adopt advanced storage infrastructure without modifying their existing code. We present our implementation, **OCPStore**, which provides high-performance, metadata-driven access to objects. OCPStore achieves up to 100,000 IOPS and a throughput of 1.5 GB/s, outperforming existing solutions by a factor of 10. Additionally, it supports parallel access to a single object and delivers a 10x speedup over prior methods.

This study examines the scheduling of electric vehicle charging at a facility managed by a coordinator. The coordinator's goal is to optimize the trade-off between user utility and operational expenses, which include fixed charges and energy procurement costs tied to power consumption. To achieve this, the paper introduces a new algorithm that combines machine learning with linear programming. This approach is benchmarked against two baseline methods: one that maximizes user utility alone and another that minimizes costs exclusively. The proposed algorithm demonstrates superior performance in balancing these objectives compared to the baselines. Furthermore, a specific variant of the algorithm is developed to address scenarios where the coordinator can only access historical data rather than real-time user information.

This study introduces new Euclidean and Hermitian self-orthogonal codes over finite fields, alongside their dual Lee and Hamming weight distributions. We present a method to derive the dual Lee and Hamming weight distributions of self-orthogonal codes from their respective dual Lee and Hamming weight distributions. Additionally, we introduce a dual Lee distance transform designed for self-orthogonal codes, which facilitates the construction of optimal self-orthogonal codes alongside optimal Euclidean and Hermitian LCD codes. The paper concludes with a comprehensive list of optimal Euclidean and Hermitian LCD codes over finite fields, organized by their dimensions and lengths.

We introduce a new method for computing the one-loop gravitational waveform of a binary system in a post-post-Newtonian framework, utilizing the recently developed method of regions to simplify the integration of loop momentum. This approach yields the waveform in terms of finite combinations of polylogarithms, where the orders are significantly reduced compared to previous calculations. We also provide closed-form expressions for the resulting waveform coefficients across various orbital configurations.

This study examines the potential of solar energy in supplying zero-carbon electricity across the American West, utilizing a linear optimization model to evaluate the optimal resource mix. The analysis indicates that achieving this goal requires portfolios that leverage solar resources, accounting for only 10% of identified high-potential development sites, thereby suggesting that viable alternatives exist outside the current selection. The research also assesses the impact of including wind energy and the advantages of solar-solar combinations, revealing that exclusive reliance on solar power necessitates a 20% increase in capacity compared to hybrid solar-wind systems. Additionally, incorporating wind power proves beneficial in certain states, whereas solar-preferring mixes offer superior results in others. Ultimately, the findings emphasize the necessity of conducting localized resource evaluations to determine the most efficient clean energy configurations.

The design of a clinical trial must commence with the establishment of estimands, the quantitative questions to be addressed, and the specific estimators required to answer them. This approach is critical for ensuring that the data collected aligns with the study's objectives. This discussion highlights the advantages of establishing estimands prior to a trial and warns against the pitfalls of defining them after the study has concluded. It further illustrates how multiple estimands can be established for a single trial, each necessitating a distinct analytical strategy.

The normalized Laplacian spectrum serves as a fundamental invariant in graph theory, playing a crucial role in network analysis. This paper presents a formula for calculating the normalized Laplacian spectrum of a graph's complement, thereby extending the findings of previous research. Additionally, we establish both upper and lower bounds for the second largest normalized Laplacian eigenvalue.

This study addresses the distributed memoryless contextual linear bandit problem, where multiple agents independently select actions within a shared environment, each receiving only its own observations. The goal is to minimize the total regret across all agents. We introduce a new algorithm that attains a regret bound of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(KT^{2/3})$, matching the optimal non-distributed linear bandit regret bound. This represents a significant improvement over the previous best-known bound of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(K^{2/3}T^{1/3})$ for distributed scenarios. Our approach relies on a communication strategy that transmits only a subset of data, specifically approximately $5d$ bits per context. This low communication cost yields substantial gains in both regret bounds and computational efficiency, surpassing existing methods that require transmitting full datasets.

The widespread adoption of machine learning in healthcare has sparked significant debate regarding the use of synthetic data as an alternative to raw information. Although synthetic datasets offer privacy and portability, they often suffer from a lack of fidelity, potentially hindering model performance. This study evaluates the impact of synthetic data quality on machine learning outcomes within the healthcare domain. We specifically examine the ability of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to produce high-quality synthetic data and compare their effectiveness against other generation techniques. Our research focuses on predicting patient readmissions using a binary classification task, utilizing a comprehensive patient cohort from a major hospital system. We assessed various models, including logistic regression, decision trees, and random forests, across three distinct synthetic datasets created using GANs and two alternative methods. Our findings indicate that GANs generate superior-quality synthetic data compared to their counterparts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the quality of synthetic data is a critical factor influencing the performance of downstream machine learning models.

This study introduces a new method for assessing the novelty and disruptiveness of scientific texts, designed to enhance the reproducibility of science reviews and meta-analyses. We developed an algorithm that integrates various indicators, such as citation frequency, references to prior work, and semantic similarity to existing texts, to generate a novelty score. We applied this approach to evaluate the novelty and disruptiveness of articles from a prominent neuroscience journal. Additionally, we conducted a user study to assess how well our automated scoring aligns with human perceptions of novelty and disruptiveness, demonstrating a strong consensus between the two.

We introduce a novel, efficient method for the spatiotemporal shaping of ultrashort pulses. This approach employs a time-dependent modulation technique driven by a "stencil" pulse; the pulse's duration matches the stencil's length. By convolving an input pulse with this stencil, the resulting output pulse achieves the desired temporal and spatial configuration. The proposed technique is highly versatile, capable of generating pulse sequences with arbitrary amplitude, phase, and time-frequency profiles. Furthermore, the method facilitates the generation of pulse trains with customizable amplitude, phase, and time delays.

The RoboCup competition, established in 1997, aims to achieve a robot playing a full football match by 2005—the 50th year following its founding. Over the past two decades, the competition has expanded significantly in scale and scope. This paper presents an overview of RoboCup, detailing its history, evolution, and future prospects.

Cross-domain recommendation systems aim to enhance prediction accuracy by leveraging user-item interactions from auxiliary domains. However, current methods often fail to fully exploit the shared underlying user-item distributions across domains, limiting their effectiveness. To address this, we introduce a dual learning model designed to jointly optimize cross-domain recommendations by aligning feature representations from both source and target domains. Our approach utilizes a dual learning framework that employs two neural networks: one for domain-specific learning and another for domain-shared learning. Additionally, we implement a dual loss function that simultaneously maximizes domain-specific and minimizes domain-shared discrepancies. Experimental results on two datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving significant improvements in both recall and AUC scores.

We introduce a class of asynchronous distributed automata operating on finite directed graphs, where each node functions as a finite-state machine capable of exchanging messages with its neighbors. We demonstrate an equivalence between this model of distributed systems and finite alternating distributed tree automata (dtrw), a variant of alternating tree automata capable of processing trees with infinite paths. Specifically, we prove that asynchronous distributed automata operating on directed graphs are sound and complete for modal logic D, which is a variant of linear-time temporal logic (LTL) featuring the "diamond" operator. We further establish that this logical equivalence holds specifically for the class of directed graphs that lack cycles.

We define a set of basic requirements for data vectors used in the study of finite group structures. Our analysis reveals that when the underlying group is not of prime power order, every finite set of vectors with finite entries can be represented as a finitely generated subgroup. Consequently, the concept of expressibility via such subgroups coincides precisely with membership in these finitely generated subgroups. We further demonstrate that for reversible vectors, expressibility achieves a stronger form: it is equivalent to linear combinations involving only integer coefficients. Finally, we establish the existence of specific vector sets for which no finitely generating subgroup can capture them.

Coronary angiography is a critical diagnostic procedure for heart disease that involves injecting a contrast medium into coronary vessels to visualize them under X-ray fluoroscopy. However, this process exposes patients to significant radiation doses, which can lead to severe complications. To mitigate these risks, fluoroscopy time is strictly minimized. Consequently, there is a pressing need for advanced algorithms capable of reconstructing high-quality angiograms from limited projection data. This study introduces a deep learning framework that utilizes a recurrent neural network (RNN) to generate angiograms from a single projection. The approach involves a deep learning model that predicts the vessel centerlines from the initial projection, followed by a second model that synthesizes the complete angiogram using the extracted centerlines. The system's efficacy was validated using a real-world dataset comprising 100 images. The results demonstrate that the proposed method successfully restores angiograms from sparse projections, achieving performance comparable to standard angiograms.

This study examines the U(1)_{\tau} model, which describes a neutrino electron-muon flavor symmetry, specifically investigating its impact on coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CE$\nu$NS). We demonstrate that within this model, the CE$\nu$NS cross section can be enhanced by a factor of 1.5 to 2 compared to the standard model prediction. This amplification arises from the presence of a large negative muon neutrino flavor eigenstate, resulting in a significant negative contribution to the cross section.

This paper examines probabilistically weak solutions to multiplicative stochastic differential equations (SDEs) driven by general Wiener processes. We establish existence and uniqueness results under conditions of local Lipschitz continuity and linear growth for the diffusion coefficient, extending and refining the work of Gao and Liang (2019). Our proof of the existence of weak solutions relies on the stochastic Feller-Kolmogorov equation, while the uniqueness argument utilizes the Girsanov transformation.

This paper introduces a new framework for NLP training that centers on objectives rather than data. By utilizing a differentiable simulation engine, we can calculate gradients for any of our objectives relative to the model's parameters, allowing us to train models directly using specific data subsets relevant to those objectives. This approach is objective-driven, offering greater flexibility and efficiency compared to traditional methods. We apply this framework to two scenarios: first, we demonstrate its use in training a language model using diverse objectives without needing a single large corpus, and second, we show how it can optimize NLP performance across multiple domains by training a single model on a combination of domain-specific data.

Traffic sign detection and classification are critical for autonomous driving systems. A comprehensive benchmark dataset is essential for developing robust algorithms that can reliably identify signs under various environmental conditions. This paper introduces the "Traffic Sign Detection and Classification Benchmark" (TSDC), a dataset comprising 1,000 images of road signs captured across diverse scenes. The collection covers multiple sign categories, lighting scenarios, and weather conditions. To ensure the dataset's validity, we conducted extensive visual inspections and data cleaning. We also evaluated the dataset using a state-of-the-art algorithm, demonstrating that TSDC effectively challenges current detection and classification methods.

Collaborative filtering (CF) has become a cornerstone of recommender systems, yet its reliance on scarce user-item interactions often leads to overfitting on negative samples and poor generalization. To address this, self-supervised CF (SCF) has emerged as a promising alternative, yet it frequently suffers from information loss and reduced efficiency due to the scarcity of available supervision. This study introduces a novel self-supervised CF framework called SS-SCF, which leverages contrastive learning to enhance representation quality. Specifically, we develop a self-supervised contrastive loss that aligns user and item representations by using masked features from the same samples. Additionally, we implement a self-supervised contrastive negative sampling strategy to mitigate the overfitting issues associated with traditional negative sampling. Comprehensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised CF methods, achieving substantial gains in both recall and area under the precision-recall curve (AUC).

We investigate the topological characteristics of a gapped Dirac semimetal model defined by two band inversion parameters, $\alpha$ and $\beta$. The system's behavior is captured by a four-dimensional topological invariant known as a 4D Chern number. By analyzing the model's behavior across various parameter values, we identify distinct phases, including 3D Chern insulators, 2D Chern insulators, Weyl semimetals, Dirac semimetals, and trivial phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the model can realize the quantum anomalous Hall effect, 3D topological magnetoelectric effects, and 3D axion insulator effects.

The discovery of gravitational waves by LIGO has marked a historic milestone, opening a new observational window into the cosmos. While current detections have been limited to the lowest mode of gravitational waves, higher-order modes (HOMs) are anticipated in future events. Detecting these modes would significantly advance astrophysics and cosmology by offering new insights into the universe's expansion and the nature of gravity. This study presents a novel method for measuring HOMs using the full data from LIGO's first observing run. By applying a Bayesian framework to a signal model that incorporates both the HOMs and noise, we estimate the posterior probability distributions for the HOMs' amplitudes. Our results indicate that the HOM amplitudes remain consistent with zero, and we establish upper limits on their values.

This study investigates the hypothesis that the gravitational influence of a currently undetected companion to the Milky Way's central black hole is responsible for the peculiar celestial motions of stars. The analysis indicates that such an external force can alter the black hole's path, causing it to move away from the galactic center and the dense stellar cluster. This displacement results in a significant shift in the calculated mass of the central black hole, rendering it substantially lower than the value derived from standard dynamical models.

Optimization is a fundamental component of numerous scientific and engineering tasks, with Gradient Descent being a widely used method for its efficiency in smooth, convex landscapes. However, in non-smooth, non-convex scenarios, Gradient Descent often suffers from slow convergence and premature local optima. Genetic Algorithms (GAs) offer a robust global optimization strategy that avoids gradient reliance, making them ideal for complex problems. This paper introduces a novel Genetic Algorithm designed to optimize the hyperparameters of a Random Forest Classifier. The study evaluates GA's performance against a state-of-the-art GA variant and a gradient-based approach. Results indicate that the new GA delivers superior convergence speed and accuracy compared to both benchmarks.

This study introduces a robust framework for hate speech detection utilizing a BERT-based model. The proposed architecture integrates data augmentation and ensemble techniques to achieve superior performance. The system's efficacy is demonstrated through results on the benchmark Hate Speech dataset, where it attains an F1-score of 0.949.

We present an extensive benchmark of the accuracy and computational cost associated with quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) forces, as a function of the effective valence charge in pseudopotentials. This evaluation spans a diverse range of materials, including ionic solids, elemental metals, and covalent compounds. The study utilizes both standard pseudopotentials and a novel, more advanced variant that incorporates nonlocal effects. QMC forces are assessed using a newly introduced metric, the "force error," which quantifies the discrepancy between the energy gradient computed with full QMC wavefunctions and that derived using a simplified wavefunction. The proposed approach is both computationally efficient and straightforward to implement. Furthermore, the force error metric is applied to evaluate the performance of various QMC approximations, such as the fixed-node approximation, the Slater determinant approximation, and the plane-wave approximation. The analysis reveals that QMC forces exhibit a highly sensitive dependence on pseudopotential quality, particularly when the effective valence charge is large. In these scenarios, standard pseudopotentials often prove insufficient, necessitating the use of the new nonlocal formulation to achieve reliable QMC forces. The study concludes by examining the QMC force error within the context of the pseudopotential approximation itself.

The 2020 U.S. presidential election saw the rapid dissemination of unsubstantiated allegations of widespread voter fraud, which severely eroded public confidence in the electoral system. This study examines the propagation of such claims on Twitter during the 2020 cycle, utilizing a novel dataset comprising 1.1 million tweets that include the hashtag #Election2020. By applying network analysis, we mapped the connections between accounts sharing these narratives and identified a core cluster of approximately 10,000 accounts responsible for disseminating more than 80% of the content. Our findings reveal that the network is highly centralized, with a core group of roughly 1,000 "hubs" driving the majority of information diffusion. Furthermore, we observed that the most active propagators were predominantly non-political users, suggesting that the rapid spread of this misinformation was fueled more by algorithmic incentives than by partisan motivations.
